h1: Bridge products: what a new distillery sells while its whisky matures
title: Bridge Products for New Distilleries | Craft Beer School
desc: Bridge products for a new craft distillery in India: gin, vodka, white spirits, RTDs and how to pick ones that fund the whisky.
teaser: Your whisky needs years. Your bank loan does not. Bridge products fill the gap.
standfirst: A new whisky distillery has to pay its bills for years before its first whisky is ready. The products it sells in the meantime keep it alive and shape how people see the brand when the whisky finally arrives.
sections:
Whisky is a slow business. Spirit goes into casks and sits for years while costs keep coming: loan payments, salaries, warehouse costs, cask purchases and excise compliance. A distillery that only makes whisky may wait three to five years or more for its first sale. Our guide to planning a craft distillery in India covers the wider plan.

Most new distilleries solve this with bridge products: spirits they can make and sell quickly using the same licence, equipment and team. Choosing the right ones is one of the most important early decisions a founder makes.

Gin is the classic choice. It needs no ageing, uses neutral spirit redistilled with botanicals and can be on shelves within months of starting production. Indian botanicals give a story: citrus, spices and herbs from your region.

The catch is competition. Craft gin has many brands in India now, so a gin needs a clear reason to exist. Design it as a product in its own right, not a filler. Many craft gin makers start from bought-in neutral spirit, where their licence allows.

Vodka is quick but hard to differentiate and often competes on price. White rum and flavoured spirits are options in some markets. Liqueurs using local fruit, coffee or spice can be distinctive and margins can be good.

Unaged grain spirit, sometimes sold as new make, can work in some markets, but rules on what it may be called vary. In many places spirit that has not been aged for the minimum period cannot be labelled whisky. Check how your state and any export market define each category before you design the label.

RTDs such as canned gin and tonic or a whisky highball made with bought-in whisky can reach younger drinkers and use the brand name widely. They need a canning or bottling line, or a contract partner. They also need close attention to shelf life, cold chain and pricing.

Check how RTDs are classified and taxed in each state you plan to sell in, as this varies and changes. A product that works in one state may be uneconomic in another.

Some new distilleries buy mature whisky from other producers, blend it and sell it under their own brand while their own spirit ages. This can bring whisky revenue early and build the brand. It must be honest. Do not imply the whisky was made at your distillery if it was not. Keep blending and labelling within the rules.

The skill of blending also prepares the team for the day their own whisky is ready. Our guide to whisky inventory planning covers how sourced and own stock fit together.

Distillery visits, tastings and shops can bring revenue and loyal fans where state rules permit visitors and on-site sales. Cask ownership schemes, where customers buy a cask of maturing spirit, are popular abroad. In India the legal position on selling casks to individuals is complex and varies by state, so take licensing advice before offering one.

Experiences also teach you who your customers are, which is valuable when the whisky launches.
Do the cash flow sums early

Before choosing products, model the years until whisky is ready. Put in production costs, excise, distribution margins and realistic sales volumes for each bridge product, month by month. Many founders find that a bridge product brings in less cash than hoped once state excise, distributor margins and listing costs are paid.

That model also shows how much whisky you can afford to lay down each year. A distillery that fills too many casks early can run out of cash before the whisky is ready. One that fills too few has little to sell when demand arrives.
Choosing bridges that help the whisky

Ask three questions of any bridge product. Does it use equipment and skills we already have? Will it sell in our markets without heavy discounting? Does it make people more likely to trust our whisky later?

A well-made gin with a clear point of view builds trust. A cheap vodka competing on price can make the brand look like a volume producer. Plan your bridges as part of the brand from the start. Budget for marketing them properly.
faqs: What should a new distillery sell before its whisky is ready?
Gin is the most common choice, because it needs no ageing. Liqueurs, RTDs, sourced blends and visitor experiences are other options where the rules allow.
Can unaged spirit be sold as whisky?
Usually not. Most rules require a minimum ageing period before spirit can be called whisky. Check your state and export market definitions.
Do bridge products hurt a whisky brand?
They can if they are cheap or unfocused. Well-made, distinctive products build trust that helps the whisky when it launches.
